title: Long-term and congenital conditions: cystic fibrosis, congenital heart disease, genomics
blurb: Explain inheritance patterns to families, apply NICE NG78 to cystic fibrosis care and recognise key nursing issues in congenital heart disease.
question: Sarah and Tom are both carriers of the cystic fibrosis gene. They ask what the chance is that their next baby will have cystic fibrosis. What should the nurse tell them?

teach.h: Living with a condition from birth
teach.body: Inherited and congenital conditions shape a child's whole life and the family's. Formally, a congenital condition is present at birth, and an inherited (genetic) condition is caused by an altered gene passed from one or both parents. Plain English: the nurse helps families understand why it happened, what the chances are next time, and how to keep the child as well as possible day to day. Cystic fibrosis (CF) and congenital heart disease (CHD) are the classic children's examples.
teach.cite: NICE NG78 Cystic fibrosis (2017); NHS Genomics Education Programme

teach.caption: Chance has no memory: the same odds apply to every pregnancy, whatever happened before.
25% has CF, 50% carrier without symptoms, 25% neither (NHS).

steps.sub: Refer to a specialist CF centre

teach.caption: Older children with symptoms such as recurrent chest infections or faltering growth are also tested.

rows.label: Infection
values: No shared rooms or bays with others

teach.h: Cross-infection: keep people with CF apart
teach.body: People with CF can pass dangerous organisms to each other. NG78 says to keep people with chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Burkholderia cepacia complex infection separate from people who do not have these infections, to separate people individually in clinics, and to give inpatients with CF individual rooms with en-suite facilities. In practice children with CF should not share a bay, a playroom session or a clinic waiting area with each other.

teach.caption: Spells happen in unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot, triggered by crying, feeding, straining, dehydration or fever.

rows.label: Low baseline SpO2 in cyanotic CHD

teach.note: Signs of CHD in a baby: blue or grey skin and lips, breathlessness, poor feeding and slow weight gain (NHS).

teach.text: A 1 in 4 chance does not mean 'one affected child in every four'. If a couple's first child has CF, the next baby's chance is still 1 in 4. Also, carriers of an autosomal recessive condition have no symptoms: being a carrier is not a mild form of the disease.

teach.h: Scenario: Noah, 5 months, during a blood test
teach.body: Noah has unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot. While crying during a blood test on the day unit he becomes deeply blue and breathless and will not settle. Nurse Kemi stops the procedure, asks his mother to hold him with his knees tucked up to his chest, gives high-flow oxygen as tolerated and calls for senior help. She records the episode and makes sure future procedures are planned to reduce distress.

items: Two carriers: 1 in 4 affected, 1 in 2 carriers, every pregnancy.
X-linked recessive: each son of a carrier mother has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected.
CF diagnosis: blood spot screen, then sweat test and gene test (NG78).
Keep people with CF apart; segregate chronic Pseudomonas or B. cepacia.
Tet spell: calm, knees to chest, oxygen, senior help. No routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental work (CG64).

summary: You can now explain recessive, dominant and X-linked inheritance to families and apply NG78 to diagnosing and caring for a child with CF. You can also manage a tet spell first-line and give accurate advice on endocarditis prevention in congenital heart disease.

A.q: Sarah and Tom are both carriers of the cystic fibrosis gene and have one son with CF. They ask the chance that their next baby will have CF. What should the nurse say?
options: 1 in 2 for each pregnancy
1 in 4 for each pregnancy
Lower now, as one child is affected
1 in 4 for daughters, none for sons
A.why: CF is autosomal recessive. With two carrier parents each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of CF, whatever happened before.

whyNot.0: 1 in 2 is the chance of a carrier, or of an affected child in autosomal dominant inheritance.
whyNot.2: Each pregnancy carries the same chance; previous outcomes do not change it.
whyNot.3: Autosomal conditions affect boys and girls equally.

A.q: Baby Amelia's newborn blood spot screening suggests cystic fibrosis. Her parents ask what happens next. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
options: A repeat blood spot at 6 weeks
A chest X-ray and lung function
A sweat test and gene test
A stool elastase test
A.why: NG78 1.1.1: after a positive newborn screen, diagnosis is confirmed with a sweat test and genetic testing at a specialist CF centre.

whyNot.0: A repeat blood spot is a screening test again; confirmation needs a sweat test and gene test.
whyNot.1: Chest imaging and lung function do not diagnose CF in a newborn.
whyNot.3: Stool elastase helps assess the pancreas but is not the confirmatory test.

A.q: Two children with cystic fibrosis are admitted on the same day. One has chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection. What is the most appropriate placement?
options: The same bay, with beds 2 metres apart
Separate bays, sharing the playroom
Next to each other for peer support
Separate single rooms, apart from each other
A.why: NG78 1.8.7: inpatients with CF should have individual rooms with en-suite facilities, and 1.8.5 keeps people with chronic Pseudomonas or B. cepacia separate from those without it.

whyNot.0: Sharing a bay allows cross-infection, whatever the distance between beds.
whyNot.1: Sharing a playroom still brings them into contact.
whyNot.2: Peer contact in person is what cross-infection guidance aims to prevent.

B.q: Maddie, 6, has cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency. Her mother says Maddie has greasy, foul-smelling stools and is not gaining weight. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Arrange review of her pancreatic enzyme dose
Advise a low-fat diet to reduce the stools
Stop enzymes and reintroduce them slowly
Reassure that this is usual in CF
B.why: NG78 1.7.6: pancreatic enzyme replacement is adjusted according to symptoms such as steatorrhoea and poor weight gain.

whyNot.1: Children with CF need a high-energy diet; restricting fat worsens weight gain.
whyNot.3: Steatorrhoea and poor growth are signs the treatment needs adjusting, not usual findings.

B.q: Ben, 4, has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive condition. Testing shows his mother is a carrier. She is pregnant with a boy. What is the chance this baby is affected?
options: 1 in 4
1 in 2
1 in 8
Almost none
B.why: In X-linked recessive inheritance each son of a carrier mother has a 1 in 2 (50%) chance of inheriting the variant and being affected.

whyNot.0: 1 in 4 applies to any child (boy or girl) of two autosomal recessive carriers.
whyNot.2: 1 in 8 is not a figure for this pattern.
whyNot.3: Sons of carrier mothers are at substantial risk, as they have only one X chromosome.

B.q: Kai, 10, had tetralogy of Fallot repaired as a baby. His father asks whether Kai needs antibiotics before his dental check-ups. What should the nurse say?
options: Yes, a single dose an hour before every visit
Yes, before any tooth extraction
Not routinely; good oral health is advised
Not routinely; use chlorhexidine mouthwash
B.why: NICE CG64: antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is not recommended routinely for dental procedures, and chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered. Advice on maintaining good oral health is given.

whyNot.0: Routine pre-dental antibiotics are not recommended under CG64.
whyNot.1: CG64 does not recommend routine prophylaxis for extractions either.
whyNot.3: Chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered as prophylaxis.

C.q: Noah, 5 months, has unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot. During a feed he becomes intensely blue, breathless and inconsolable. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Lie him flat and raise his legs
Hold him with knees to chest and give oxygen
Give a 10 mL/kg fluid bolus first
Continue the feed to calm him down
C.why: First-line tet spell care is supportive: calm the child, place them knees to chest (often on a parent's lap) to raise systemic vascular resistance so less blood bypasses the lungs, give high-flow oxygen and call for senior help.

whyNot.0: Lying flat with the legs raised does not raise systemic resistance the way the knee-chest position does.
whyNot.2: A fluid bolus comes later if the spell persists after positioning, oxygen and medication.
whyNot.3: Feeding is a known trigger; continuing it may worsen the spell.

C.q: Leila, 3, has palliated cyanotic heart disease. Her usual SpO2 is 78–82% in air. On the ward her PEWS chart scores the saturation. A student suggests not scoring it as it is normal for her. What should the nurse do?
options: Leave the saturation unscored on the chart
Score it and use the agreed escalation plan
Record it as 95% to reflect her normal
Stop measuring SpO2 as it is unhelpful
C.why: National PEWS has no derogation for children with low baseline saturations: they still score. Escalation should follow the chart and any individual plan agreed by the cardiology team.

whyNot.0: National PEWS does not allow saturations to go unscored for a low baseline.
whyNot.2: Recording a false value is a documentation error and unsafe.
whyNot.3: SpO2 trends remain important for detecting deterioration in cyanotic heart disease.

C.q: Jordan, 11, has CF. His mother asks why his annual review now includes a test for diabetes. What is the best explanation?
options: NG78 advises yearly CF-related diabetes testing from 10
CF causes type 1 diabetes in most teenagers
His enzymes raise blood glucose over time
It is checked because he is overweight
C.why: NG78 1.7.24: test for CF-related diabetes annually from the age of 10.

whyNot.1: CF-related diabetes is a distinct condition, not type 1 diabetes in most teenagers.
whyNot.2: Pancreatic enzymes do not cause diabetes.
whyNot.3: Testing is age-based in CF, not weight-based.

reteach.title: Odds, sweat and separation
reteach.question: What three facts do families of a child with CF most often ask about?

blocks.body: Odds: two carriers have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child in every pregnancy. Diagnosis: newborn blood spot, then sweat and gene tests. Daily life: airway clearance, enzymes adjusted to stools and weight, yearly diabetes checks from 10, and staying apart from other people with CF to prevent cross-infection.

blocks.text: Two children with CF are not company for each other on a ward. Peer support should happen in ways that keep them physically apart.

explain.body: Autosomal recessive: the child needs an altered gene from both parents; two carriers have a 1 in 4 chance each pregnancy. Autosomal dominant: one altered copy is enough, so an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of passing it on. Boys and girls are equally affected in both.

test.q: Aisha has neurofibromatosis type 1, an autosomal dominant condition. Her partner is unaffected. What is the chance each of their children inherits it?
options: 1 in 4
1 in 2
1 in 8
Sons 1 in 2, daughters none
test.why: An affected parent with an autosomal dominant condition has a 1 in 2 chance of passing it on to each child.

whyNot.0: 1 in 4 applies to two carriers of a recessive condition.
whyNot.2: 1 in 8 is not a figure for this pattern.
whyNot.3: Autosomal conditions affect sons and daughters equally.

explain.body: The altered gene is on the X chromosome. Boys have one X, so a son of a carrier mother has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected. Daughters have a 1 in 2 chance of being carriers; some carriers have mild features. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the classic example.

test.q: A carrier of an X-linked recessive condition asks about her daughter's risk. What is correct?
options: 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier
1 in 2 chance of being severely affected
1 in 4 chance of being a carrier
No chance of carrying the gene
test.why: Each daughter of a carrier mother has a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier.

whyNot.1: Daughters are usually carriers rather than severely affected.
whyNot.2: 1 in 4 is the recessive affected figure, not this one.
whyNot.3: Daughters can inherit the X carrying the variant.

explain.body: Diagnosis by blood spot, then sweat and gene test. rhDNase is the first-choice mucoactive treatment. Enzymes are adjusted to symptoms. Yearly diabetes testing from 10. Segregate people with chronic Pseudomonas or B. cepacia.

test.q: Which statement about cystic fibrosis care matches NICE NG78?
options: Diabetes testing begins at 16
Children with CF should share bays
Enzyme doses are fixed for life
rhDNase is the first-choice mucoactive
test.why: NG78 recommends rhDNase as the first-choice mucoactive agent.

whyNot.0: CF-related diabetes testing is yearly from age 10.
whyNot.1: People with CF should be kept apart to prevent cross-infection.
whyNot.2: Enzyme doses are adjusted according to symptoms.

explain.body: Signs in babies include blue or grey skin and lips, breathlessness, poor feeding and slow weight gain. Tet spells need calm, knee-chest position and oxygen. CG64: no routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures, no chlorhexidine mouthwash, but good oral health matters.

test.q: Which is a recognised trigger of a hypercyanotic spell in a baby with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot?
options: Sleeping in a cool room
Sucking on a dummy
Crying or straining
Being held by a parent
test.why: Crying, feeding, straining, dehydration and fever are recognised triggers of hypercyanotic spells.

whyNot.0: A cool sleeping room is not a recognised trigger.
whyNot.1: Calm sucking on a dummy is not a recognised trigger.
whyNot.3: Being held, especially knees to chest on a parent's lap, helps end a spell rather than trigger one.
